extracted.intended_audience: researchers in empirical aesthetics / neuroaesthetics, psychologists studying aesthetic judgment, and mathematicians interested in mathematical beauty
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of the aesthetic appeal of mathematical equations, comparing domain experts (mathematics students) and laypeople using behavioral methods (Q-sort, self-report) and statistical measures of agreement and drivers of preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for equations that are familiar to the observer (Hypothesis 2a). Experts were on average more familiar with the equations, and both groups preferred familiar equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure familiarity via post-task self-report per equation (participants indicate which equations they knew prior). Analyze both within-subject median assignments (e.g., pile numbers) and group-level counts (number of participants familiar with each equation). Correlate number familiar per equation with average aesthetic categorization (Spearman’s rho) and compare correlations across groups (Fisher’s z). Use t-tests to compare familiar vs unfamiliar assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning / Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgments driven by the extent to which the observer understands the relationships the equation denotes (Hypothesis 2b). Experts reported meaning as a driver more often than laypeople.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask participants to indicate whether 'meaning' informed their classification (binary checkbox or rating). Examine group differences (Chi-squared tests) and relate reported use of meaning to Q-sort results to test whether understanding predicts higher aesthetic ratings, especially among experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity (count of elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complexity operationalized as number of elements in an equation (count of numbers, Latin letters, Greek letters, mathematical signs, and total elements). Hypothesis 2c explored its effect on aesthetic judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify complexity by counting elements per equation. Correlate this count with average aesthetic categorization (Spearman’s rho). Compare correlations across groups (experts vs laypeople) and test significance (Fisher’s z). Note: experts in this study preferred equations with fewer elements (negative correlation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity as an explicit criterion for aesthetic appeal (listed option on participant criterion form), historically associated with mathematical beauty and elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide 'simplicity' as an option for participants to endorse. Use binary checked/not checked responses to determine whether simplicity influenced sorting. Consider measuring simplicity both as subjective endorsement and via objective counts (e.g., element count) to relate perceived simplicity to measured complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance as a possible contributor to the aesthetics of equations (included among provided classification options).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include 'balance' as an explicit checklist item for participants to indicate whether it informed their judgments. Analyze endorsement frequencies by group and cross-tabulate with Q-sort placement to assess influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetry included as an option participants could select when reporting what influenced their classification of equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect symmetry as a binary reported criterion. Use endorsement rates and correlations with aesthetic rankings to evaluate its role, particularly relative to other factors (meaning, familiarity, complexity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Form (visual/formal layout) presented as a potential driver of aesthetic judgment (checkbox option).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask participants whether 'form' guided their sorting. Compare endorsements across experts and laypeople to determine whether form (a sensorial/visual factor) is weighted differently by expertise level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition (overall arrangement/organization of elements within the equation) listed among factors participants could endorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat composition as a reported criterion (checked/not checked). Analyze how composition endorsements relate to Q-sort placements and whether composition correlates with other measurable visual features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensorial / Visual Features (shape, relative size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory/visual properties of equations (shapes, relative sizes of numbers and symbols) that may drive aesthetic judgments, particularly for laypeople who rely more on sensorial qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider extracting objective visual features (e.g., symbol shapes, spacing, relative sizes) or include participant-report items about sensorial impressions. Expect laypeople to weight these features more heavily; compare with expert reliance on meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Aesthetic Sensitivity (VAST)
rubrics_metrics.description: General visual aesthetic sensitivity measured by the Visual Aesthetic Sensitivity Test (VAST) to control for baseline aesthetic ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administer VAST (or equivalent) before main task to ensure groups do not differ in general aesthetic sensitivity. Compare VAST scores across groups (t-tests) to rule out general taste differences as confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement / Consensus (reliability measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of agreement among participants as an index of shared aesthetic judgment (Cronbach’s alpha, Chi-squared tests). The study predicted greater agreement among experts (Hypothesis 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal-consistency measures (Cronbach’s alpha) computed on Q-sort data and Chi-squared tests for categorical agreement to compare groups. Higher alpha indicates greater consensus; report statistical significance of group differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q-Sort Technique (forced distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the Q-Sort technique to force a normal distribution of relative rankings (two-step sorting: coarse 3-pile then fine 9-pile distribution) for assessing relative aesthetic preferences and agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a two-round Q-sort: first sort into 'unaesthetic / neither / aesthetic' with no limits, then redistribute into nine piles with predetermined counts (e.g., 3,5,7,10,14,10,7,5,3). Use this forced distribution to make participant rankings comparable and to compute measures of agreement and relative preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic Triad Components
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework that aesthetic experience emerges from interaction of three systems: knowledge-meaning, sensory-motor, and emotion-valuation; used to interpret differential contributions for equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating equations, consider and (if possible) measure the relative contributions of knowledge-meaning (domain knowledge/understanding), sensory-motor (perceptual features), and emotion-valuation (reward/affective response). Expect knowledge-meaning to dominate for experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual Fluency
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis that aesthetically pleasing equations may be processed more fluently; fluency here driven by meaning and understanding rather than solely sensory qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess processing fluency indirectly (e.g., reaction times, ease ratings) or infer from correlations between familiarity/meaning and aesthetic ratings. Use established fluency frameworks (Reber et al., 1998) to interpret results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/Shared Taste (invariance among mathematicians)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that mathematicians from different cultures agree on aesthetic valuation of mathematical concepts, indicating some degree of cultural invariance in mathematical beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generalizing results, consider cross-cultural sampling or cite literature on shared taste among mathematicians. Use measures of inter-subject agreement to quantify shared taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus Selection (representative range)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select stimuli (equations) across a wide range of mathematical subfields and degrees of perceived beauty as judged by an expert to ensure variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult domain experts (e.g., a mathematics professor) when selecting equations. Use a sufficiently large and diverse stimulus set (the study used 64 equations) to sample the space of possible aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting Reported Criteria via Checklist (binary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask participants to state which criteria they considered (provided options such as simplicity, balance, complexity, symmetry, form, composition, meaning) using a binary checked/not checked approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a limited set of theoretically informed options plus an 'other' option for free responses. Use the binary endorsements to estimate which factors were consciously considered during sorting and to compare across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural Controls: Time limit and two-step sorting
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural choices (one-hour maximum, two-step sorting) intended to make the task manageable and comparable across participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose a reasonable time limit and use an initial coarse sort before the fine Q-sort to help participants complete the task. Pilot these parameters to ensure feasibility and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical Approach: Correlational and comparative analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic procedures used to link drivers (familiarity, meaning, complexity) with aesthetic categorization (Spearman’s rho, t-tests, Chi-squared, Fisher’s z comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute within-group correlations between driver measures and average aesthetic rankings (Spearman’s rho for nonparametric associations). Use paired-sample and independent-sample t-tests to compare assignments and familiarity, Chi-squared tests for endorsement frequencies, and Fisher’s z to compare correlation strengths between groups.
